claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a supersaturated FCC matrix with a fine, non-equilibrium microstructure.
The starting material contains additive-manufacturing-induced defect sites such as intrinsic edge dislocations.
At elevated temperature, gas environment governs degradation by modifying surface and near-surface chemistry.
An oxidizing atmosphere forms a non-adherent, Cr-rich oxide scale on the target alloy.
Formation of the oxide scale consumes Cr and produces near-surface Cr depletion in the FCC matrix.
Cr depletion undermines the intrinsic ductility of the FCC matrix.
Oxidizing exposure promotes brittle intermetallic or sigma-like precipitates, preferentially at grain boundaries.
The precipitation of sigma-like phases is triggered specifically by oxidation-induced Cr depletion.
Reducing or low-oxygen exposure suppresses oxide formation relative to oxidizing exposure.
Under reducing conditions, additive-manufacturing-induced defects concentrate internal stress and promote alternative phase transformations.
Defect-mediated stress accumulation or phase transformation under reducing conditions causes a sharp loss of ductility and catastrophic failure.
Relative to an inert baseline, oxidizing exposure will cause marked near-surface Cr depletion.
Relative to an inert baseline, oxidizing exposure will produce discernible brittle secondary phases.
Oxidizing exposure will significantly degrade tensile and creep performance relative to an inert baseline.
Reducing exposure will reduce ductility and eventually cause failure despite minimized oxide formation.
Inert-atmosphere exposure at the same temperature and duration will cause minimal oxidation and Cr depletion.
The FCC matrix will retain its initial mechanical performance after the inert-atmosphere exposure.
The proposed behavior applies at approximately 800–1000 °C for exposures longer than 100 hours.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that both oxidizing and reducing conditions can substantially degrade mechanical behavior through different pathways, but the falsification rule treats an absence of a marked mechanical-property difference between those two conditions as disproof. Similar mechanical losses would remain compatible with the stated two-pathway hypothesis.
